# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological advances, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the success of DES in reducing restenosis, concerns persist regarding permanent metallic implants, including chronic inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, impaired vasomotion, and the risk of very late stent thrombosis [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support during vessel healing and subsequently resorb, theoretically restoring vascular physiology [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, clinical evidence, complications, and current standing of BVS in contemporary PCI.

## Rationale and Device Characteristics

The central concept underpinning BVS is that the role of a coronary stent is temporary—required only during the early phase of vessel remodeling and healing [4,5]. Once this period passes, a permanent implant may become a liability. By dissolving over time, BVS could allow restoration of vasomotor tone, late luminal enlargement, and freedom from a permanent metallic cage [5,6].

The most extensively studied device was the Absorb everolimus-eluting bioresorbable vascular scaffold (Abbott Vascular), composed of a poly-L-lactide backbone with a poly-D,L-lactide coating eluting everolimus [6,7]. Other platforms included magnesium-based scaffolds (Magmaris) and various polymeric designs [8,9]. Early imaging and first-in-man studies (ABSORB cohort A and B) demonstrated feasibility, with evidence of scaffold resorption and recovery of vasomotion at follow-up [7,10].

## Clinical Evidence

Initial enthusiasm was supported by promising early outcomes. The ABSORB cohort studies and subsequent registries suggested acceptable safety and efficacy in selected lesions [10,11]. The pivotal ABSORB II, ABSORB III, ABSORB Japan, and ABSORB China trials compared the Absorb BVS with the Xience cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent [12,13,14,15].

ABSORB III, the largest randomized trial, demonstrated non-inferiority for target lesion failure at one year [13]. However, longer-term follow-up revealed troubling signals. ABSORB II failed to meet its co-primary endpoints, showing no superiority in vasomotion and worse late lumen loss with BVS [12]. Pooled and meta-analytic data revealed increased rates of device thrombosis, particularly very late scaffold thrombosis, compared with metallic DES [16,17,18].

The AIDA trial independently confirmed higher rates of definite or probable device thrombosis with Absorb BVS in routine practice [19]. Meta-analyses consolidated these findings, demonstrating a significantly elevated risk of scaffold thrombosis and target vessel myocardial infarction [17,18,20].

## Mechanisms of Failure

Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the adverse outcomes. The thicker struts of the Absorb scaffold (approximately 150 μm versus <90 μm for modern DES) promoted flow disturbance and delayed endothelialization [21,22]. Suboptimal implantation technique—including inadequate lesion preparation, undersizing, and lack of high-pressure post-dilatation—contributed substantially to early and late events [22,23]. Late scaffold discontinuities and intraluminal dismantling during the resorption process were identified by intravascular imaging as substrates for very late thrombosis [24,25].

Recognition of these issues prompted refinement of implantation technique, encapsulated in the "PSP" (predilatation, sizing, post-dilatation) protocol, which improved outcomes in observational analyses [23,26]. Nonetheless, these measures could not fully overcome the inherent limitations of the first-generation device [26].

## Current Status and Future Directions

In light of accumulating safety concerns, Abbott withdrew the Absorb BVS from the commercial market in 2017 [27]. Subsequent extended follow-up of randomized trials showed that the excess risk of adverse events was largely confined to the resorption period, with convergence of event rates after approximately three years [28]. This temporal pattern reinforced the importance of scaffold design and bioresorption kinetics.

Despite the setback, interest in resorbable technology persists. Newer-generation scaffolds with thinner struts, improved mechanical properties, and faster resorption are under development [29]. Magnesium-based scaffolds have shown favorable preliminary results, and ongoing trials aim to determine whether next-generation devices can deliver the theoretical benefits of resorption without the safety penalties of the first generation [8,29,30].

## Conclusion

BVS represented an ambitious attempt to overcome the limitations of permanent metallic stents by providing transient scaffolding followed by complete resorption [4,30]. While early data were encouraging, robust randomized evidence revealed an unacceptable risk of scaffold thrombosis attributable to device design and implantation technique [17,19]. The withdrawal of the Absorb scaffold tempered initial optimism but yielded valuable lessons [27]. The concept of bioresorption remains scientifically compelling, and improved second-generation devices may yet fulfill the original promise—provided they demonstrate safety across the full resorption timeline in adequately powered trials [29,30].
